```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(SMSD)
# Three decimal places for numbers written into the text.
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

## The Research Question

An education researcher is evaluating whether a supplemental tutoring
program improves achievement relative to standard instruction. The
effect size is the standardized mean difference, &delta; =
(&mu;<sub>1</sub> &minus; &mu;<sub>2</sub>) / &sigma;, the difference
between the two population means in units of the common standard
deviation (Kelley, 2007; Kelley & Rausch, 2006). The researcher wants to
report how large the effect is, with a confidence interval narrow enough
to be informative. Designing a study around the width of the confidence
interval, and not around the outcome of a significance test, is the
accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) approach (Maxwell, Kelley, &
Rausch, 2008).

Fixed sample size AIPE planning (`DMAR::ss_aipe_smd()`) requires a
planning value for &delta;. When no defensible planning value exists,
the sequential procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018)
applies: data are collected in stages, and a stopping rule decides when
the confidence interval for &delta; is no wider than a target the
researcher has chosen. The procedure is distribution free; it does not
assume that the scores are normal.

## The Method

With <em>n</em> observations in each group, &delta; is estimated by
<em>d</em> = (<em>M</em><sub>1</sub> &minus; <em>M</em><sub>2</sub>) /
<em>s</em><sub>p</sub>, the difference between the sample means divided
by the pooled standard deviation (Equation 24 of the article). The
sampling variance of <em>d</em> is approximately the asymptotic variance
divided by <em>n</em>. The asymptotic variance (xi squared in the
article) depends on the two means, the common variance, and the third
and fourth central moments of the two populations. The procedure
estimates it from the data without assuming a distribution; the
estimate is the row `xi_squared` of the result and is written `V`
below. With `width` for the target full width (omega in the article)
and `z` for the standard normal quantile of the confidence level, the
procedure has three parts.

* **The pilot sample size** is the larger of a minimum (`m_0`, 4 by
  default) and `ceiling(2 * z / width)` (Equation 21).
* **The stopping rule** is met at the first <em>n</em>, at or after the
  pilot sample size, with `n >= (4 * z^2 / width^2) * (V + 1 / n)`
  (Equation 22). The term `1 / n` is a correction that keeps the rule
  from being met too early.
* **The confidence interval** runs from `d - z * sqrt(V / n)` to
  `d + z * sqrt(V / n)` (Equation 28). Whenever the rule is met its
  width is at most `width`.

## Workflow

The researcher commits to a target full width of 0.50 at the 95%
confidence level, computes the pilot sample size, collects the pilot
sample, and checks the stopping rule. The data here are simulated from
a population with &delta; = 0.50; in a real study each call to
`new_tutored()` or `new_standard()` is a new group of students.

```{r workflow-pilot}
set.seed(113)
new_tutored <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0.50, sd = 1)
new_standard <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = 0.50, conf_level = 0.95)
m

tutored <- new_tutored(m)
standard <- new_standard(m)
out <- seq_aipe_smd(tutored, standard, width = 0.50, conf_level = 0.95)
out
```

The row `criterion_n` is the right side of the stopping rule, rounded
up, and the limits are the interval described above. Both can be
reproduced from the other rows:

```{r workflow-rule}
z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - 0.95) / 2)
d <- out$value[out$term == "smd"]
V <- out$value[out$term == "xi_squared"]
n <- out$value[out$term == "current_n"]

ceiling(4 * z^2 / 0.50^2 * (V + 1 / n))
d + c(-1, 1) * z * sqrt(V / n)
```

The rule is not met at the pilot, so the study goes on: students are
added to each group, five at a time here, and the rule is checked again
after each addition, until it is met.
`vignette("step-by-step-sequential-workflow", package = "SMSD")` writes
that loop out. To show where it leads, the rest of the study is
simulated here in one piece, 200 more students per group in the order
in which they would have been recruited, and `seq_path()` applies the
check at every stage the study would have reached.

```{r workflow-path}
tutored <- c(tutored, new_tutored(200))
standard <- c(standard, new_standard(200))

path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_smd, list(group_1 = tutored, group_2 = standard),
                 width = 0.50, conf_level = 0.95, by = 5)
path
```

```{r workflow-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Two panels. Top: the estimated standardized mean difference with its confidence interval against the sample size per group; the interval narrows as students are added, the stopping point is marked, and the stages after it are drawn in gray. Bottom: the current sample size rising through the criterion sample size, which stays between about 125 and 150; the two cross at the stopping point."}
plot(path)
```

```{r workflow-values, include = FALSE}
final <- summary(path)
covers <- final$lower_limit <= 0.50 && 0.50 <= final$upper_limit
```

The rule was first met at `r final$stop_n` students per group, and that
is where a study run as planned stops. The students simulated beyond
that point are there only to complete the picture; they are drawn in
gray in the plot, and an estimate from a later stage may not be reported
in place of the one at the stopping point. At the stopping point the
estimate is `r f3(final$estimate)`, with a 95% confidence interval from
`r f3(final$lower_limit)` to `r f3(final$upper_limit)`. The width,
`r f3(final$upper_limit - final$lower_limit)`, is within the target, and
the interval `r if (covers) "contains" else "does not contain"` the
population value of 0.50. The check at the stopping point is stored with
the path as `attr(path, "final_check")`, and `seq_report()` writes the
result up:

```{r workflow-report}
seq_report(path)
```

## The Correction to Equation 26

Equation 26 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, p. 232) gives
the asymptotic variance of the standardized mean difference, and the
sample version printed under their Equation 27 is what the stopping
rule uses.
As printed, both omit a factor of one half in the term that carries the
third central moments. With &mu;<sub>k3</sub> and &mu;<sub>k4</sub> for
the third and fourth central moments of group <em>k</em>, the printed
equation is

> asymptotic variance = 2 &minus; (&mu;<sub>1</sub> &minus;
> &mu;<sub>2</sub>)(&mu;<sub>13</sub> &minus; &mu;<sub>23</sub>) /
> &sigma;<sup>4</sup> + [(&mu;<sub>1</sub> &minus;
> &mu;<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup> / (4 &sigma;<sup>6</sup>)]
> [(&mu;<sub>14</sub> + &mu;<sub>24</sub>) / 4 &minus; &sigma;<sup>4</sup>
> / 2]

and the corrected equation, which the package implements, is

> asymptotic variance = 2 &minus; (&mu;<sub>1</sub> &minus;
> &mu;<sub>2</sub>)(&mu;<sub>13</sub> &minus; &mu;<sub>23</sub>) / (2
> &sigma;<sup>4</sup>) + [(&mu;<sub>1</sub> &minus;
> &mu;<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup> / (4 &sigma;<sup>6</sup>)]
> [(&mu;<sub>14</sub> + &mu;<sub>24</sub>) / 4 &minus; &sigma;<sup>4</sup>
> / 2].

The two agree when the means are equal and when the two groups have the
same third central moment, which includes every pair of symmetric
distributions; for normal data both reduce to 2 + &delta;<sup>2</sup> /
4. They differ when the means differ and the groups are skewed
differently. The authors' derivation of the corrected equation is
posted at
<https://kenkelley.org/wp-content/uploads/articles/Kelley_Darku_Chattopadhyay_Equation_26.pdf>,
and the same document is installed with the package, at the path that
`system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD")` returns:

```{r eq26-file}
file.exists(system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD"))
```

A case in which the two forms differ shows which one describes the
data. Take two populations with unit variance and a standardized mean
difference of 0.5, one right skewed (a standardized chi square
distribution with 3 degrees of freedom, with skewness &radic;(8/3) and
kurtosis 7) and the other its mirror image. With unit variances the
third and fourth central moments are the skewness and the kurtosis.

```{r eq26-forms}
xi_squared <- function(delta, skew_1, skew_2, kurt_1, kurt_2, half) {
  2 - half * delta * (skew_1 - skew_2) +
    (delta^2 / 4) * ((kurt_1 + kurt_2) / 4 - 1 / 2)
}
skew <- sqrt(8 / 3)
printed <- xi_squared(0.5, skew, -skew, 7, 7, half = 1)
corrected <- xi_squared(0.5, skew, -skew, 7, 7, half = 1 / 2)
c(printed = printed, corrected = corrected)
```

If the asymptotic variance divided by <em>n</em> is the sampling
variance of <em>d</em>, then <em>n</em> times the variance of <em>d</em>
across many samples should be close to the asymptotic variance. Four
thousand samples of 200 per group:

```{r eq26-simulation}
set.seed(113)
n <- 200
reps <- 4000
row_var <- function(m) rowSums((m - rowMeans(m))^2) / (ncol(m) - 1)

x <- 0.5 + matrix((rchisq(reps * n, df = 3) - 3) / sqrt(6), nrow = reps)
y <- -matrix((rchisq(reps * n, df = 3) - 3) / sqrt(6), nrow = reps)
d <- (rowMeans(x) - rowMeans(y)) / sqrt((row_var(x) + row_var(y)) / 2)

n * var(d)
```

```{r eq26-values, include = FALSE}
simulated <- n * var(d)
se_simulated <- simulated * sqrt(2 / (reps - 1))
```

The simulated value, `r f3(simulated)` (Monte Carlo standard error about
`r f3(se_simulated)`), agrees with the corrected form,
`r f3(corrected)`, and not with the printed one, `r f3(printed)`. The
variance estimate that `seq_aipe_smd()` computes from a large sample of
the same two populations is an estimate of the corrected quantity:

```{r eq26-package}
big_x <- 0.5 + (rchisq(50000, df = 3) - 3) / sqrt(6)
big_y <- -(rchisq(50000, df = 3) - 3) / sqrt(6)
big <- seq_aipe_smd(big_x, big_y, width = 0.10)
big$value[big$term == "xi_squared"]
```

A reader who applies the printed equation to data like these would
compute a criterion sample size less than half of what the corrected
equation gives, and an interval too narrow by a factor of about
`r round(sqrt(corrected / printed), 1)`.

## When the Estimate Is Not Yet Usable

The variance estimate is a difference of terms built from sample
moments, and in a very small sample that difference can come out zero or
negative even though the quantity it estimates is positive. A check on such a
sample looks like this. The scores are ratings from a pilot of five
per group at a target width of 0.80.

```{r unusable}
rating_1 <- c(7, 6, 6, 7, 6)
rating_2 <- c(5, 3, 4, 5, 5)
early <- seq_aipe_smd(rating_1, rating_2, width = 0.80)
early
attr(early, "variance_unusable")
```

No variance has been estimated, so there is nothing from which to build
an interval or a criterion. The check says so in four ways: the limits
are `NA`; `criterion_n` is above `current_n`; the attribute
`variance_unusable` is `TRUE`; and a note under the result says what
happened. The stopping rule is reported as not met, so a loop written
on `attr(out, "is_satisfied")` keeps sampling without any special
handling. The row `xi_squared` shows the lower bound
<em>n</em><sup>&minus;3</sup> (here 5<sup>&minus;3</sup> = 0.008), not
an estimate.

This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed. The
article bounds the variance estimate below by
<em>n</em><sup>&minus;3</sup> (its Equation 27), and the printed rule
would use that bound in place of a zero or negative estimate. The
consequence is easy to compute for this sample:

```{r unusable-printed-rule}
z <- qnorm(0.975)
4 * z^2 / 0.80^2 * (5^-3 + 1 / 5)
2 * z * sqrt(5^-3 / 5)
```

The right side of the rule is just under 5, so the rule would be met at
once with 5 per group, and the interval would be
`r f3(2 * z * sqrt(5^-3 / 5))` wide where 0.80 was requested: a study
that stops at its pilot and reports a precision it does not have. The
package uses the bound as the article prescribes whenever the estimate
is positive, however small, and treats an estimate that is zero,
negative, or not finite as what it is, no estimate yet. The same rule
applies across the package's check functions (see "An Unusable Variance
Estimate" in `help("SMSD-package")`).
<!-- not from a help page: 0.80 -->

With more data the estimate becomes usable and the rule is evaluated in
the ordinary way:

```{r unusable-later}
rating_1 <- c(rating_1, 5, 7, 6, 4, 6)
rating_2 <- c(rating_2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 4)
seq_aipe_smd(rating_1, rating_2, width = 0.80)
```

For the standardized mean difference this situation is uncommon at the
widths studies use. It arose above because the pilot was very small and
the ratings take few distinct values. In the simulations of continuous
data reported in `?seq_aipe_smd` (a population value of 0.5, target
widths of 0.4 and 0.2, normal and right skewed data) the variance
estimate was never zero or negative, and at a width of 0.8 with normal
data that happened in fewer than 1 study in 1,000
(`?seq_aipe_sensitivity`).
It is common for some other effect sizes at wide targets,
the correlation and the regression slope above all, and
`vignette("seq-aipe-correlations", package = "SMSD")` gives the
figures. A second, rarer case is reported the same way: when neither
group shows any variation the estimate itself cannot be computed, and
the check carries a note that says so.

## What the Procedure Guarantees

The width is at most the target whenever the rule is met. That holds in
every sample. The coverage of the interval approaches the confidence
level as the target width narrows and the final sample grows (Theorem 4
of the article); it is an asymptotic property. How good the
approximation is at a given width depends on the population value and
on the distribution of the scores. In simulations of the procedure as
shipped, with a population value of 0.5 and one observation per group
added at each stage, 95% intervals contained the population value in
0.952 of studies at a target width of 0.4 (6,000 studies, about 200 per
group at the end) and in 0.946 at a width of 0.2 (2,000 studies, about
790 per group) for normal data, and in 0.944 and 0.949 for right skewed
data (`?seq_aipe_smd`). At a width of 0.8, where a study ends with
about 51 per group, coverage was still 0.95 for normal data
(`?seq_aipe_sensitivity`). For right skewed data at that width it is
two to three hundredths lower. It is lower again at targets wider
still, for normal data as well, and the more so the larger the
population value.

`seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity()` runs the procedure many times for a
population value, width, batch size, and distribution (normal or right
skewed) of the user's choosing, and reports the final sample size and
the coverage to expect;
`vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD")` describes its
output and runs the skewed case just mentioned. When each
observation has a price and the goal is the smallest total cost of
sampling and estimation error, `seq_mr_smd()` is the procedure to use
(`vignette("mrpe-smd", package = "SMSD")`).
